title: REO Disposition and Marketing Standards — CTL Policy
content:
REO Disposition Policy — Clear-To-List Requirements for REO Property Marketing and Sale.

Purpose: Real Estate Owned (REO) properties are properties that have been acquired by a lender or servicer through foreclosure, deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, or forfeiture. The disposition of REO requires careful coordination of legal clearance, property preparation, pricing strategy, and marketing compliance. This policy establishes the standards for REO properties progressing through the CTL gate.

Section 1 — Acquisition Path Verification:
Verify the method by which the property became REO: (a) Foreclosure sale — trustee's deed or sheriff's deed recorded in the name of the lender, servicer, or their nominee. (b) Deed-in-lieu (DIL) of foreclosure — voluntary conveyance by the borrower, documented by a recorded deed and a DIL agreement. For DIL acquisitions, verify that the borrower executed the deed voluntarily and that any conditions of the DIL agreement (such as borrower relocation timeframe) have been satisfied. (c) Forfeiture — court-ordered transfer, such as in bankruptcy proceedings. Verify the court order is final and non-appealable.

Section 2 — First Look Period:
Many investors and regulatory programs require a first-look period before REO properties are made available to investor buyers. During the first-look period, only owner-occupant buyers, government entities, and designated nonprofits may submit offers. Common first-look programs include: FHA First Look (15 days for HUD REO), Fannie Mae First Look (20 days for Fannie REO), and Freddie Mac First Look (20 days for Freddie REO). Servicers managing REO for these entities must comply with the applicable first-look period. The CTL process should identify whether a first-look period applies and set the appropriate marketing restrictions.

Section 3 — Marketing Requirements:
REO properties must be marketed through channels that provide broad market exposure. Standard marketing requirements include: (a) listing on the local Multiple Listing Service (MLS) through a licensed real estate broker, (b) listing on the asset owner's approved marketing platform (such as the auction platform), (c) professional-quality exterior and interior photographs (minimum 15 photos), (d) accurate property description including bedroom/bathroom count, square footage, lot size, and condition disclosures, and (e) clear identification of the sale type (REO, as-is, etc.).

Section 4 — Pricing Strategy:
The list price for an REO property should be established based on the current BPO or appraisal, adjusted for property condition and local market dynamics. Pricing strategies include: (a) List at BPO value — standard approach for properties in average condition. (b) List below BPO value — may be used for properties in poor condition, in markets with high inventory, or when rapid disposition is prioritized. (c) Auction pricing — starting bid may be set at a discount to attract competitive bidding. The CTL process does not dictate pricing strategy but ensures that a current, non-stale valuation exists to inform the pricing decision.

Section 5 — As-Is Sale Terms:
Most REO properties are sold on an as-is basis, meaning the seller makes no warranties regarding property condition. However, as-is does not exempt the seller from disclosure obligations. Known material defects must still be disclosed per state law. The as-is designation affects the CTL process in that property condition issues (non-hazardous) generally do not block listing — they are managed through disclosure and pricing adjustment rather than repair.

Section 6 — Bulk Sale Considerations:
When a portfolio of properties is being considered for bulk sale rather than individual listing, the CTL determination for each property should still be completed. Properties that fail individual CTL may still be included in a bulk sale at appropriate discount. The CTL report for each property should note any deficiencies that would affect the bulk sale pricing.

Section 7 — Disposition Timeline Standards:
Industry standard disposition timelines from acquisition to listing: Non-judicial foreclosure states: 30 to 60 days. Judicial foreclosure states: 45 to 90 days. CWCOT properties: per HUD timeline requirements. Properties exceeding these disposition timelines should be escalated for review. Extended holding times increase property preservation costs, tax liability, and the risk of vandalism or deterioration.

Section 8 — Compliance and Fair Housing:
All REO marketing and disposition activities must comply with the Fair Housing Act (42 USC Sections 3601-3619). REO properties must be marketed without discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability. Marketing materials, showing policies, and offer evaluation criteria must be applied uniformly. Equal Housing Opportunity logos and statements must be included in all marketing materials.

References: Fair Housing Act (42 USC Sections 3601-3619). FHA/Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac first-look program guidelines. Industry standard REO disposition practices.
